title: Acid–base concepts
competency: Define acids and bases by the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts, identify conjugate pairs and amphiprotic species.

keywords.def: A substance that increases [H⁺] (H₃O⁺) when dissolved in water.
A substance that increases [OH⁻] when dissolved in water.
Two species that differ by exactly one H⁺, such as HF and F⁻.
Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
A molecule or ion that can donate or accept a proton, depending on its partner.
A species that accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
A species that donates an electron pair to form a bond.

en.text: Arrhenius defined acids and bases by what they do in water. An acid increases [H⁺] (really H₃O⁺); a base increases [OH⁻]. Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄) and strong bases (Group 1 hydroxides, Ca, Sr and Ba hydroxides) ionize completely. The idea fails outside water and for bases such as NH₃ that contain no OH.

am.text: አርሄኒየስ አሲድ በውሃ ውስጥ [H⁺] ይጨምራል፤ ቤዝ [OH⁻] ይጨምራል። ሀሳቡ ከውሃ ውጭ እና እንደ NH₃ ላሉ ቤዞች አይሠራም።

screens.title: Lemon or soap?
screens.ask: Almaz dips blue litmus paper into four liquids. Which one turns it red?
screens.after: Lemon juice contains citric acid. Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.

screens.title: Arrhenius acids and bases
paras: An acid increases [H⁺] in water. A base increases [OH⁻].
H⁺ never exists alone in water. It joins H₂O to form H₃O⁺.
Strong acid: ionizes completely. HClO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + ClO₄⁻.
Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄.
Strong bases: Group 1 hydroxides and Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂.
Neutralization: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

screens.title: Where Arrhenius fails
paras: It works only in water.
NH₃ and Na₂CO₃ make water basic but contain no OH⁻ to release.
It cannot explain HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s), which happens without water.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A substance that increases [H⁺] (H₃O⁺) when dissolved in water.
A substance that increases [OH⁻] when dissolved in water.

screens.title: Classify by Arrhenius
screens.why: Acids add H⁺ to water; bases add OH⁻; NaCl adds neither.
screens.clue: What ion does each give in water?

screens.text: A bare H⁺ ion moves freely in water.
screens.why: H⁺ is a tiny bare proton. It bonds at once to H₂O, forming H₃O⁺.
screens.clue: What happens when a proton meets a lone pair on water?

screens.text: Which is a drawback of the Arrhenius concept?
opts: It cannot explain why NH₃ is a base
It cannot explain why HCl is an acid
It cannot explain why NaOH is a base
It cannot explain neutralization in water
screens.ans: It cannot explain why NH₃ is a base
screens.why: NH₃ has no OH⁻ to release, yet its solution is basic.
screens.clue: Look for the base without OH in its formula.

screens.text: Which reaction can the Arrhenius concept NOT describe as acid–base?
screens.why: There is no water and no OH⁻: Arrhenius cannot call it acid–base.
screens.clue: Which one happens in the gas phase?

ideas.name: Brønsted–Lowry acids, bases and conjugate pairs

en.text: Brønsted and Lowry (1923) defined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, in any medium. When an acid gives up H⁺ it becomes its conjugate base; when a base takes H⁺ it becomes its conjugate acid. The partners differ by one H⁺. The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base, and reactions favour the weaker acid and weaker base.

am.text: ብሮንስቴድ–ሎውሪ፡ አሲድ ፕሮቶን ሰጪ፣ ቤዝ ፕሮቶን ተቀባይ ነው። ተጓዳኝ ጥንዶች በአንድ H⁺ ይለያያሉ። ጠንካራ አሲድ ደካማ ተጓዳኝ ቤዝ አለው።

screens.title: Who gives the proton?
screens.ask: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which reactant gives away a proton (H⁺)?
screens.after: H₂O loses H⁺ and becomes OH⁻; NH₃ gains it and becomes NH₄⁺. Here water acts as an acid.

screens.title: Proton donors and acceptors
paras: Acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor.
Water is not needed.
NH₃ is a base because it accepts H⁺ from water.
Every Arrhenius acid is also a Brønsted–Lowry acid.

screens.title: Conjugate pairs
paras: Acid − H⁺ → its conjugate base. Base + H⁺ → its conjugate acid.
The conjugate base has one fewer H and one more minus charge.

screens.title: Strength of conjugate pairs
paras: The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
HCl is strong, so Cl⁻ is a negligible base.
Reactions go mainly toward the weaker acid and weaker base.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Two species that differ by exactly one H⁺, such as HF and F⁻.

screens.text: The conjugate acid of HPO₄²⁻ is
screens.why: Add one H⁺: HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺ → H₂PO₄⁻ (charge −2 + 1 = −1).
screens.clue: Add exactly one H⁺ and fix the charge.

screens.title: Match each acid with its conjugate base
screens.why: Remove one H⁺ and add one minus charge.
screens.clue: One fewer H, one more minus.

screens.text: In OCl⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HOCl + OH⁻, the Brønsted–Lowry acid is
screens.why: H₂O gives H⁺ and becomes OH⁻.

screens.text: Which is NOT a conjugate acid–base pair?
screens.why: They differ by two H⁺. The pairs are H₃O⁺/H₂O and H₂O/OH⁻.
screens.clue: Count the H atoms in each pair.

screens.text: Ka: HF 7.2 × 10⁻⁴, HNO₂ 4.5 × 10⁻⁴, HCN 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰. Base strength, strongest first:
screens.why: The weakest acid (HCN) has the strongest conjugate base.
screens.clue: Reverse the order of the acids.

screens.title: Put these bases in order, strongest first
screens.why: Their conjugate acids, weakest first: H₂O, NH₄⁺, CH₃COOH, HNO₃, HCl.
screens.clue: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base.

en.text: Some species can donate or accept a proton depending on their partner: they are amphiprotic. Water is the most important one; HCO₃⁻ and H₂PO₄⁻ are others. In autoionization two identical molecules transfer a proton: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ and 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻.

am.text: አምፊፕሮቲክ ዝርያዎች እንደ አጋራቸው ፕሮቶን ይሰጣሉ ወይም ይቀበላሉ፤ ውሃ ዋናው ምሳሌ ነው። 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻።

screens.title: Acid or base?
screens.ask: Water reacts with NH₃ and with CH₃COOH. What role does water play?
opts: A base with CH₃COOH, an acid with NH₃
screens.after: Water accepts H⁺ from acetic acid but gives H⁺ to ammonia. It depends on its partner.

screens.title: Autoionization
paras: Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion.
Water: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
One molecule acts as an acid, the other as a base.
Liquid ammonia: 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻.

screens.title: Amphiprotic species
paras: They can donate or accept a proton.
HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O: HCO₃⁻ is an acid.
HCO₃⁻ + HF → H₂CO₃ + F⁻: HCO₃⁻ is a base.
Other examples: H₂O, H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻, HS⁻.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
A molecule or ion that can donate or accept a proton, depending on its partner.

screens.why: Each has an H to give and a lone pair or negative charge to take H⁺. NO₃⁻ and CH₃COO⁻ only accept; HNO₃ only donates.
screens.clue: Look for species with a removable H AND room for one more.

screens.text: When H₂PO₄⁻ acts as a base, it becomes
screens.why: A base gains one H⁺: H₂PO₄⁻ + H⁺ → H₃PO₄.

screens.text: The self-ionization of liquid ammonia is
screens.why: One NH₃ gives H⁺ (→ NH₂⁻), the other takes it (→ NH₄⁺), like 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
screens.clue: Same pattern as water, no water involved.

screens.text: In liquid ammonia, the strongest base that can exist is
screens.why: Any stronger base would take H⁺ from NH₃ and become NH₂⁻, just as OH⁻ is the strongest base in water.
screens.clue: Think of the solvent minus one H⁺.

en.text: Lewis defined acids and bases by electron pairs. A Lewis base donates an electron pair; a Lewis acid accepts one to form a bond. Look for a lone pair (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, Cl⁻) and an empty orbital (B in BF₃, metal ions, CO₂, H⁺). The Lewis idea is the broadest: every Brønsted–Lowry reaction is also a Lewis reaction.

am.text: ሉዊስ ቤዝ የኤሌክትሮን ጥንድ ይሰጣል፤ ሉዊስ አሲድ ይቀበላል። ይህ ትርጉም ከሦስቱ ሰፊው ነው።

screens.title: No proton moves
screens.ask: BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃. No H⁺ moves. Is this an acid–base reaction?
opts: Yes: NH₃ shares its lone pair with B
screens.after: NH₃ donates an electron pair to the boron atom, which has only six valence electrons. That is a Lewis acid–base reaction.

screens.title: Electron pairs
paras: Lewis base: donates an electron pair to form a bond.
Lewis acid: accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
B in BF₃ has only 6 valence electrons: it has room for a pair.
Look for a lone pair (base) and an empty orbital (acid).
Negative ions and molecules with lone pairs: bases. Cations and electron-poor molecules: acids.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A species that accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
A species that donates an electron pair to form a bond.

screens.text: In BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃, the Lewis acid is
screens.why: B accepts the lone pair from N.
screens.clue: Which atom has an empty orbital?

screens.title: Match each reaction with its Lewis acid
screens.why: The acid accepts the electron pair; the partner with the lone pair is the base.
screens.clue: Find the species with room for an electron pair.

screens.text: In CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃, the Lewis base is
screens.why: O²⁻ in CaO gives an electron pair to the C of CO₂.
screens.clue: Which species has the lone pair?

screens.text: Which statement about Lewis bases is NOT true?
opts: Lewis bases donate an electron pair
screens.why: Bases are molecules with lone pairs or anions. Cations are usually Lewis acids.
screens.clue: Which species have spare electron pairs?

screens.text: Which is a Lewis acid but NOT a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
screens.why: BF₃ has no H⁺ to donate, but B accepts an electron pair.
screens.clue: A Brønsted–Lowry acid must have an H to give.

notes.text: Exercise 1.1 a and c: the book's equations are unbalanced (2Br⁻, 2OH⁻). Correct: HBr + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Br⁻; NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻.
p.8: "CH₃COO⁻ is a strong base" is wrong; acetate is a weak base (Chart 1.1 lists it as weak). It is only stronger than Cl⁻.
p.4: the strong Group IIA hydroxides are usually Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂ (Mg(OH)₂ is only slightly soluble).
Review Part I Q1 is missing "not": "a Brønsted–Lowry base but NOT an Arrhenius base" (answer NH₃).
